name: Augustan Satire and the Scriblerans
description: The high satire of Pope, Swift, Gay and their friends, directed against dullness, pedantry, enthusiasm and the corrupt public life of the new Augustan age.
historical_context: Written in the party warfare after 1710, when the Swift-led Examiner and the Addison-led Spectator fought for the political centre, and codified in the Scriblerus Club (c. 1714), whose members were Pope, Swift, Gay, Arbuthnot, Parnell and Atterbury. The failure of the Jacobite rising of 1715 and the triumph of the Whig oligarchy pushed the mode from party attack to a wider diagnosis of cultural decay, and the Licensing Act of 1737 and the Case of the Five Bishops (1731) drove much of the later work into verse and closet form.
aesthetic_principles: Horatian and Juvenalian precedent; ridicule as a weapon against imposture; the couplet as the vehicle of judgment; decorum, good sense and the 'correctness' of the ancients; the conviction that dullness is a moral as well as an aesthetic offence.
defining_characteristics: Mock-epic and the lowered sublime; the personified abstraction (Dulness, Criticism, Bufo); the persona and the mask; the verse epistle and the dialogue; the learned parody and the forged critical apparatus; sustained prose invective in an ironised first person.
historical_significance: It set the standard of English prose and verse satire for the next century, created the modern idea of the critic as a public moralist, and left a body of political and cultural commentary (A Modest Proposal, The Dunciad) that remains the period's most quoted description of itself.

name: The Spectator and Periodical Journalism
description: The daily and weekly essay papers that created a new middle-rank reading public and a model of familiar, civilized prose.
historical_context: The Tatler (1709) and The Spectator (1711-12, revived 1714) exploited the new circulation of coffee-house and tea-table reading, the growth of the provinces, and the removal of the press-licensing Act in 1695, which left writers answerable to law rather than to the Stationers' censors. The form was carried forward by Steele's Guardian, Tavern Project and Englishman, Addison's Freeholder, the idler papers of the mid-century, Johnson's Idler and Rambler, and the Lady's Magazine and Monthly Review of the 1780s.
aesthetic_principles: Instruction joined to pleasure; the avoidance of party abuse; a 'middle state' of style between the scholastic and the vulgar; the polite essay as a rehearsal of everyday moral judgment; the mask of a club, a spectator, or a persona.
defining_characteristics: Short prose essays on manners, marriage, taste, commerce, death and the theatre; the club as a fictional society of disagreeing types (the knight, the merchant, the fellow-guard, the beauty); letters to the editor; the recurring character sketch; the mixture of allegory, quotation and domestic observation.
historical_significance: It fixed the prose style taught to English schoolchildren for two centuries, made periodical writing a profession, and created the reading public to which the novel, the review and the sermon all subsequently addressed themselves.

name: The Rise of the English Novel
description: The emergence, between Robinson Crusoe and The Rivals, of extended realistic prose fiction as the dominant form of the period.
historical_context: The expansion of a literate middle rank, especially of women readers; the cheap circulation of the three-volume library novel after 1770; the Copyright Act of 1710 and its 1741 revision, which made authorship a marketable profession; the decline of aristocratic patronage; and the philosophical empiricism of Locke and the moral-sense theorists, which made particular experience and the history of the passions respectable subjects of serious writing.
aesthetic_principles: Verisimilitude and 'nature'; the historian or editor persona claiming documentary truth; the moral probation of private individuals; probability, particularity and time; the reader's sympathetic identification as the mechanism of instruction.
defining_characteristics: Formal plurality: the autobiography, the journal, the epistolary sequence, the picaresque journey, the editor's compilation, the mock-chivalric romance, the tale of terror; large casts drawn from the social middle; open plots of advancement, seduction or ruin; long citation of letters and documents.
historical_significance: It made prose fiction the central form of English literature and the principal vehicle of social analysis, moral inquiry and, later, of the arguments about gender, marriage and slavery that the century opened.

name: Neoclassical Criticism and the Rules
description: The critical language of taste, decorum, the ancients and the general, developed by Rymer, Addison, Pope, Dennis, Johnson and the academic rhetoricians.
historical_context: Rymer's tracing of the French neoclassical dramatic rules back to Aristotle, the Battle of the Books, the Addisonian rehabilitation of Milton, the quarrels over Homer and over the unities, and the institutionalization of rhetoric and belles-lettres in the universities and in Blair's and Home's lectures gave the period a self-conscious critical vocabulary which its own writing constantly tests.
aesthetic_principles: Imitation of nature by imitation of the ancients; the rules as empirical generalizations from the practice of the best writers; decorum, propriety and the removal of exceptions; taste as a social faculty; judgment over fancy.
defining_characteristics: The verse epistle and the critical essay; the preface as criticism; the character of an author; comparative judgment of the ancients and moderns; the analysis of the sublime, wit, and genius; the dictionary, glossary and chronology as critical instruments.
historical_significance: It created modern literary criticism and literary history in English, and its quarrels - about unities, about blank verse, about Homer and Ossian - formed the terms on which romantic theory later defined itself.

name: Topographical and Estate Poetry
description: Descriptive verse in couplets that surveys a landscape, a country seat, a river or a distant view, and reads it as moral, historical and political evidence.
historical_context: The remodelling of country houses and their parks after 1700, the culture of the Grand Tour and the picturesque, the Whig language of liberty and independence attached to landed property, and the publication of local histories and maps gave the form its social occasion. Denham's Cooper's Hill (1642) had set the pattern; Pope's Windsor Piece (1713), Thomson's Seasons (1726-30) and the later estate poems develop it.
aesthetic_principles: The view as argument; description subordinated to moral and political reflection; the 'living landscape' of taste and improvement; the station of the poet as a freeholder surveying a nation.
defining_characteristics: Heroic couplets with a topographical sweep; the actual named place as structure; the passage from prospect to reflection to panegyric; the inset of history, commerce and agriculture; the seasonal and weather writing that Thomson introduces.
historical_significance: It supplied the descriptive vocabulary later used by Cowper, Crabbe, Wordsworth and the Victorian topographers, and it is the form in which the century thought about property, improvement and national identity.

name: The Graveyard School and Preromantic Meditation
description: Long blank-verse meditations on death, obscurity, night, the ruin and the humble dead, which prepare the romantic lyric.
historical_context: The funeral and mourning culture of the mid-century, the vogue for ruins and abbots, the expansion of the parish cemetery and the burial-ground, the influence of Young's Conjectures on Original Composition (1759), and the translation of German and French melancholy writing created the taste; Blair's grave-yard poem and Whitehead's Roman tomb give it its political and academic variants.
aesthetic_principles: Melancholy as a valuable discipline; the sublime of darkness and of the dead; the apostrophic address; the education of feeling by the contemplation of mortality; obscurity and gloom preferred to the clarified day.
defining_characteristics: Unrhymed five-beat lines; the night, the churchyard, the yew, the tombstone, the worm and the dust; the speaker's solitary progression toward a religious or philosophical conclusion; the apostrophe to an abstraction or an unknown dead person; the fragment and the collected short poem.
historical_significance: It supplied the eighteenth century's most persistent imagery of selfhood and death, formed the vocabulary of Gothic fiction, and handed the blank-verse meditation to Cowper and to Wordsworth.

name: Sentimentalism and the Culture of Feeling
description: The moral and literary movement that located virtue in the capacity to feel, and made sympathy, tenderness and the painful pleasure of distress the tests of character.
historical_context: Derived from the moral-sense philosophy of Shaftesbury, Hutcheson and Hume and from the empiricism of Locke's school, and diffused through the sermons of Brown, the plays of Colman and Kelly, the novels of Mackenzie and the later Richardson, the essays of the Sentinel and the Spectator, the poetry of the Task and Goldsmith's deserted village, and the periodical literature of the 1770s and 1780s.
aesthetic_principles: Fellow-feeling as the evidence of virtue; the tear and the palpitation as authentic signs; distress and poverty as the trial of the heart; benevolence as religion; a morality of motive rather than of station.
defining_characteristics: The scene of tested distress; the sensitive poor man, the feeling prostitute, the benevolent traveller; apostrophe and exclamation; the interruptive address to the reader's own sensibility; a syntax of half-finished sentences and suspended feeling.
historical_significance: It produced the sentimental and the 'feeling' novel, the cult of the pathetic in the theatre, the language of abolitionist appeal, and the first sustained feminist argument from the shared capacity to feel; and it was the target of Austen's, and of the ironists', first modern critique.

name: The English Enlightenment and Deist Controversy
description: The rational examination of revelation, miracle, church authority and moral obligation, carried on in tracts, sermons, histories and encyclopedic prose.
historical_context: Toleration (1689) and the lapse of the licensing Act made controversy a printed trade; the Boyle Lectures, the productions of the freethinking press, Collins, Woolston, Morgan, Tindal and the Deists met with the replies of Butler, Law, Waterland, Stillingfleet and the high-church party, while Hume's posthumous dialogues and Gibbon's history extended the sceptical enquiry to providence itself and to the rise of Christianity.
aesthetic_principles: The appeal to evidence, analogy and the 'light of nature'; the historical and philosophical reading of Scripture; the separation of morality from revealed religion; irony and the sober reductio as the instruments of attack.
defining_characteristics: The treatise and the reply; the free argument on miracle and prophecy; the deist schematic Christianity 'old as the creation'; the historical criticism of the biblical books; the philosophical essay on religion and the afterlife; the ironised defence.
historical_significance: It established the historical and critical study of religion in English, forced the church into a reasoned apologetic, and set the terms on which nineteenth-century faith and doubt, and the modern study of the Bible, were argued.

name: The Scottish Enlightenment
description: The cluster of philosophical, historical and economic writing produced in Edinburgh and Glasgow, which recast the theory of society, of commerce and of the human mind.
historical_context: The Union of 1707, the prosperity of the tobacco merchants, the teaching system of the Scottish universities and the clubs and societies of Edinburgh (the Select Society, the Mirror, the Poker Club) concentrated durable enquiry on the question of how societies progress through the stages of hunting, pastoral, agricultural and commercial life.
aesthetic_principles: The empirical and conjectural history of society; the moral sense and sympathy as the basis of obligation; commercial interdependence as the source of civility and of its dangers; the essay and the lecture as the forms of public philosophy.
defining_characteristics: The treatise of political economy; the four-stages theory of society; the philosophical history and the historical essay; the rhetorical and aesthetic lectures; the medical, juridical and antiquarian dissertation; the society and the journal as media.
historical_significance: It supplied the theoretical language of political economy and of sociology, influenced the American founding and the British reformers, and reshaped the English essay, novel and travel book with theories of sympathy, progress and commercial society.

name: The Bluestockings and Women's Letters
description: The learned social circles of women and their literary correspondence, translation, criticism and pedagogy, which made female intellectual company a public institution.
historical_context: The assemblies of Elizabeth Vesey and Elizabeth Montagu in the 1750s, the gift of Montagu's 'blue stocking' nickname, the growth of female readership and of the circulating library, the improvement of girls' education, and the example of the French salonnières gave women a recognised, if mocked, cultural role; the same decades produced the first sustained arguments for women's education and for women's civil existence.
aesthetic_principles: Conversation and correspondence as serious forms; the union of erudition and civility; translation as scholarship; the moral and social usefulness of letters; the defence of female learning against ridicule.
defining_characteristics: The familiar letter and the letter of criticism; the conversation piece and the commonplace book; translation from Greek, Italian and French with scholarly annotation; the conduct and education book; the essay on taste; the plays and poems of the professional woman writer.
historical_significance: It created a visible tradition of women's intellectual writing in English, formed the institutional model of the literary society, and prepared Wollstonecraft's vindication and the nineteenth-century woman of letters.

name: The Evangelical Revival and Hymn Writing
description: The Methodist and Calvinistic revival and its devotional verse, which made experimental religion and congregational song a major literary fact.
historical_context: The 'Aldersgate experience' of John Wesley (1738), Whitefield's open-air preaching, the field-sermons and the connexion, the growth of Methodist societies and bands, the dispute over predestination between Wesley and Whitefield, and the printing networks of the Revival - the Weekly Circular and the Arminian Magazine - created a mass devotional literature, while Newton's and Hart's hymns served the Calvinistic interest.
aesthetic_principles: Plainness, intelligibility and doxological function; the meter and the tune as carriers of doctrine; experience, not ornament, as the warrant; the hymn as sermon and as prayer.
defining_characteristics: The metrical psalm and hymn; the journal and the narrative of conversion; the sermon printed for society use; the spiritual diary; the doctrinal dispute in verse and prose; the account of a religious experience.
historical_significance: It supplied the English language with some of its most durable hymn texts, registered in literature the experience of the labouring and middling ranks, and provided the religious vocabulary later tested by Wordsworth, Newman and the Victorians.

name: Garrick and the Regenerated London Theatre
description: The management of Drury Lane and Covent Garden, the reform of acting and of the repertoire, and the dramas written for it, from The Beggar's Opera to The Rivals and Pizarro.
historical_context: The theatrical patents, the Licensing Act of 1737, which confined new play-writing to the two patent houses, the burletta and the afterpiece as evasions of that monopoly, the retirement of the old company, David Garrick's management of Drury Lane from 1747, the Shakespeare jubilee at Stratford (1769), the removal of the audience from the stage, the new lighting and the painted prospect, and the rise of the actor as a public celebrity.
aesthetic_principles: Nature and effect; the actor's body and voice as the medium; the revival and adaptation of the old repertoire; sentimental comedy against 'laughing comedy'; the prologue, epilogue and jubilee as the theatre's own occasional poetry.
defining_characteristics: The domestic tragedy, the musical drama, the comic opera, the farce and the afterpiece; the adaptation and 'restoration' of Shakespeare; the prologue and epilogue; the theatrical pamphlet and the memoir; the play of sensibility and the play of ridicule.
historical_significance: It established the actor-manager, the repertory system and the modern idea of Shakespeare on the stage, and it made the theatre the chief arena in which sentimental and anti-sentimental theories of the passions were fought out.

name: Primitivism, the Bardic Revival and Ossian
description: The vogue for 'primitive' poetry: the Celtic forgeries and translations of Macpherson, the Chatterton rows, the ballad collections, and the theory of original genius.
historical_context: The defeat of the '45 and the annexation of the Highlands, the antiquarian and literary society, the publication of James Macpherson's Fragments of Ancient Poetry (1760) and the poems of Ossian, the quarrel with Ireland and with the English critics, the rediscovery of Chatterton's Rowley poems, and Percy's Reliques made the supposed primitive, the popular and the native the subject of a national debate about the origin and value of poetry.
aesthetic_principles: The primitive as authentic and the polished as debased; genius without rules; the fragment, the invocation and the song as original forms; national and popular antiquity as evidence; enthusiasm and the dark sublimate.
defining_characteristics: The prose-poetic fragment with a scholarly apparatus of dissertations and notes; the imitated 'ancient' hymn and battle-poem; the collected and edited popular ballad; the forged or attributed early text; the controversy tract and the antiquarian disquisition on authenticity.
historical_significance: It created a European cult of primitive poetry, transformed the theory of genius, revived the study of the ballad and of northern antiquity, and gave romanticism - in England, Germany and France - a large part of its imagery and its self-conception.

name: Abolitionist and Anti-Slavery Writing
description: The pamphlets, sermons, poems, narratives and speeches that made the slave trade a subject of English public argument and produced the first published slave narratives.
historical_context: The Atlantic trade and the plantation economy, the growth of the Black population of London, the Somerset judgment (1772), the Quaker and evangelical campaigns, Benezet's and Granville Sharp's tracts, the Test Case of the Zong massacre controversy, the publication of Equiano's narrative (1789) and the formation of the Society for the Abolition of the Slave Trade in the year of the French Revolution.
aesthetic_principles: Testimony and evidence; the appeal to shared feeling and to natural right; the exposed body of the sufferer as argument; the documentary and autobiographical warrant against the abstract calculation of commerce.
defining_characteristics: The narrative of a life held and recovered; the sermon on the trade; the parliamentary and legal argument; the poetical address and the medal-inscription; the enquiry into population and produce; the slave's own first person.
historical_significance: It introduced into English literature the testimony of enslaved people as published autobiography, founded the humanitarian campaign that abolished the trade in 1807, and set the enduring literary problems of empire, race and testimony.

name: Gothic and the Literature of Terror
description: The revived romance of haunted castles, tyranny, pursuit and supernatural dread, and its popular and critical offshoots.
historical_context: The taste for ruins, Catholic and 'romantic' antiquity, the quarrel over the value of terror, the three-volume circulating-library novel, the success of Walpole's Castle of Otranto as a model, the vogue of the Italian and Spanish scene, the anti-Catholic and the reformist readings of the monk story, and the reaction against French classical tragedy.
aesthetic_principles: The sublime of terror and of obscurity; the suspension of belief engineered by the marvelous; the machinery of prophecy, manuscript and ruin; the machinery of feeling: horror, sympathy and the faint.
defining_characteristics: The haunted castle, abbey and labyrinth; the tyrant, the usurper and the persecuted maiden; the found manuscript and the editorial frame; the explained supernatural and its residue; the long sentence of alarm, exclamatory dialogue and interpolated song.
historical_significance: It made terror a commercial and critical genre, produced the first historical novel, and gave the nineteenth century - from Mary Shelley and the Brontës to the sensation novel - its characteristic plots and settings.
